title: Robert Smalls: He Stole a Confederate Ship

segments.text: Hello, and welcome to Black History in 10 Minutes, from The Black History Room.
Every episode, one true story that history tried to forget, told in about ten minutes.
So get comfortable, and let's begin.
Today: the man who took a Confederate ship, and sailed his family to freedom.

Before dawn on May the thirteenth, 1862, an enslaved man put on the captain's straw hat, stood at the wheel of an armed Confederate steamer, and sailed it straight past the guns of Fort Sumter. On board were sixteen people. And Smalls had made a grim promise: if they were caught, they would sink the ship rather than surrender.
His name was Robert Smalls. And by the end of his life, he had served five terms in the United States Congress.
Robert Smalls was born into slavery on April the fifth, 1839, in Beaufort, South Carolina. His mother, Lydia Polite, was enslaved too, and Robert grew up in the shadow of their enslaver's house.

When he was about twelve, he was sent to Charleston and hired out. He lit the city's street lamps. He worked on the docks, as a rigger and a sailor. But the money he earned was not his. Most of his wages went to his owner.

Year by year, he learned the water. The tides, the channels, the sandbars of Charleston harbor. He became so skilled that he was steering ships, doing the work of a pilot, the job the law would never give him the title for.
In 1856, he married Hannah Jones, an enslaved woman who worked in Charleston hotels. They started a family.

And Robert tried to do it the legal way. He asked what it would cost to buy his wife and their little daughter. The answer was about eight hundred dollars. He had saved about one hundred. At that rate, it could take him most of his life. And at any moment, his family could be sold away from him.
So he started to think about another way out.

It would mean risking everything. If the plan failed, the men could lose their lives, and their wives and children could be sold away. He would need the right ship, the right night, and nerves of steel.

When the Civil War began, Smalls was working aboard a Confederate steamer called the Planter. It carried guns, ammunition and supplies around Charleston harbor. Smalls was its wheelman. He knew the ship, the harbor, and every signal the captain gave to pass the forts.

On May the twelfth, 1862, the Planter took on four big guns from a dismantled fort, along with ammunition. That evening, the three white officers went ashore for the night, as they often did, leaving the ship to the enslaved crew. It was the chance Smalls had been waiting for.

Around three in the morning, the crew fired up the boilers and slipped away from the wharf. They stopped at another wharf to pick up their families, including Hannah and the children. Sixteen people were now aboard.

Then they headed for the harbor mouth, past fort after fort: Castle Pinckney, Fort Johnson, Fort Moultrie. Smalls put on the captain's straw hat, folded his arms, and stood the way the captain stood, so that from a distance, in the dark, he would look like him. At each fort, he gave the right whistle signals. And one after another, the forts let them pass. At about half past four in the morning, they steamed past Fort Sumter itself.

Once they were out of range, the crew pulled down the Confederate flag and raised a white bedsheet. As the sun came up, they steered for the Union ships blockading the harbor. In the morning fog, the crew of the U.S.S. Onward saw a Confederate steamer coming straight at them. They swung a gun toward the Planter and were about to fire, when someone shouted that he could see a white flag. Robert Smalls handed over the Planter, its guns, and its cargo to the United States Navy.
Sixteen people had gone to sleep enslaved. By sunrise, they were free. And the Union had gained not only a ship, but a man who knew every channel, fort and mine in Charleston harbor.
The news spread across the North. Harper's Weekly put Smalls's face in its pages. Congress passed a bill to reward him and his crew, and Smalls received fifteen hundred dollars.

And what Smalls carried in his head was worth as much as the ship. He knew the channels, the forts, and where the mines were laid. Within days, Union forces used what he told them to take positions near Charleston that the Confederates had abandoned.

And he did more than escape. The Union general in the region sent Smalls to Washington, with a message for President Lincoln and the Secretary of War: let Black men fight. Soon after, the Secretary of War authorized up to five thousand Black soldiers to be raised in the area.

Smalls went back to the war, this time on the Union side. He piloted the Planter and the ironclad Keokuk in at least twelve engagements. In one battle, under heavy fire, the white captain lost his nerve, and Smalls took command and brought the ship to safety. Afterward, he was made the Planter's captain.

Even as a war hero, he was not treated as an equal. In December 1864, in Philadelphia, he was thrown off a streetcar reserved for white passengers. He joined a mass boycott. And in 1867, a new law opened Philadelphia's streetcars to Black passengers.

After the war, Robert Smalls went home to Beaufort. And he bought the house where he had been enslaved. The boy who had grown up in the shadow of that house now owned it. Imagine walking through the front door of a house you were once only allowed to serve in.

He opened a store, and a school for Black children. In 1868, he helped write a new constitution for South Carolina. He served in the state house, then the state senate. And in 1875, he took his seat in the United States House of Representatives. Over the years, he served five terms in Congress.
But Reconstruction did not last. White supremacists took back power in South Carolina, and set out to take the vote away from Black citizens.

In 1895, South Carolina held a convention to write a new constitution, designed to strip Black men of the right to vote. Robert Smalls was one of only six Black delegates. He stood up and spoke against it. He said of his people: All they need is an equal chance in the battle of life. He lost that vote. But he did not stay silent.

He served for years as the collector of customs at the port of Beaufort, until 1913. And on February the twenty-third, nineteen fifteen, Robert Smalls died, in the house where he had once been enslaved. He was seventy-five years old.

A boy whose wages belonged to someone else. A father who could not afford to buy his own family. A man who took a warship, sailed past Fort Sumter, and came home to own the house where he had been enslaved.

That's the story of Robert Smalls. Thank you for listening to Black History in 10 Minutes, from The Black History Room. If this story meant something to you, follow the show, and share it with someone who should hear it. And if you'd like to help us keep these stories coming, you can support us on Ko-fi, at ko-fi dot com, slash, the black history room.
Next time: a baby who was traded for a horse, and grew up to become one of the most famous scientists in America. Until then, keep history alive.
